text: It's been fine, thanks. Revising graph problems and finishing my final year project.

Nice, sounds like a busy final year. Let's get started properly then. This round runs for about thirty minutes: a short intro from you, then a coding problem where I'll want you thinking aloud, and we'll finish with some time for your questions. To kick off, give me a short introduction of your background and the work you've done.

I'm a final year computer science student at Bennett University. Last year I interned on a micro frontend dashboard in TypeScript and React, and I built a side project called Relay that lets me control my laptop from my phone.
Good, that's a clear picture. Tell me a bit more about Relay — what does it do under the hood, and what was the trickiest technical decision you had to make while building it?

On the internship I worked on the shell that loads other teams' remotes with Module Federation, and I wrote the shared login and token refresh. The tricky part was concurrent refreshes, so I made one in-flight refresh promise that all remotes wait on.
That's a solid pattern — a single in-flight promise so concurrent 401s don't trigger a refresh storm. So who consumes that shared promise, the remotes themselves or the shell's HTTP layer?
The shell's HTTP layer. Remotes just call a shared fetch wrapper, and when it sees a 401 it awaits the single refresh and retries the request, so the remotes never touch the token logic.
Good, that's a clean separation — token concerns live in one place. Alright, let's move to the coding problem. I'm putting it on your screen now; have a read and tell me how you'd approach it.

text: Thanks. A couple of things: how does the team handle releases and on-call, and what would you expect a new grad to be shipping in their first few months?

On releases, teams here deploy independently — small, frequent changes with feature flags rather than big release trains, and a rollback path ready before anything ships. On-call, engineers do carry a rotation for the services they own, and it can be heavy during busy periods; people are honest that work-life balance varies with the quarter, so it's worth asking specifics for the team you'd join. A new grad typically starts by shipping small, well-scoped changes to an existing service with a mentor reviewing, then picks up their own tickets once they've shown they can take something end-to-end.
